Customer Gateway Configuration

Prepare the AWS CGW resource and the matching on‑prem IPsec device settings so tunnels form reliably and routing works without manual intervention.

In this lesson

What AWS requires for a CGW, when to use static routing vs BGP, the IPsec Phase 1 and 2 parameters your device must match, and common troubleshooting checks.

Why it matters

A correct CGW and device configuration prevents tunnel failures, avoids routing blackholes, and enables automated failover when you use BGP.

screens.title: What is a Customer Gateway (CGW)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Customer Gateway is a logical resource you create inside AWS to tell the platform where your on‑prem VPN device is and how it will behave. It does not perform encryption itself; the physical or virtual VPN appliance in your data center does that work. In practice, the CGW holds a small set of fields: the public IP address reachable from the internet, a BGP ASN if you plan to use dynamic routing, and an optional device name to help operators identify it. Why use a CGW resource? AWS needs to know the remote endpoint to allocate tunnel endpoints, produce configuration files, and establish the two independent IPsec tunnels that provide redundancy. A common misconception is treating the CGW as the tunnel — it’s not. Think of the CGW as a directory entry: it allows AWS to target the actual tunnel negotiations to your device. A concrete example: when you create a CGW with a public IP of 203.0.113.10 and ASN 65001, AWS will use that IP to start IKE negotiations and, if BGP is used, expect a BGP neighbor formed with the VGW. Key takeaway: keep the CGW's public IP stable and accurate; changing it will break existing tunnels and require reconfiguration.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is a Customer Gateway?
Definition

Customer Gateway: logical AWS resource

Represents your physical or software VPN device so AWS can form VPN tunnels and provide configuration details.

Core fields
  • Public IP address (must be reachable)
  • BGP ASN for dynamic routing or placeholder for static
  • Device name for operator clarity
Concrete example
Create a CGW with public IP 203.0.113.10 and ASN 65001 so AWS can generate tunnel settings and a config file tailored to your device.
Key Takeaway

The CGW tells AWS where to connect and whether BGP will be used; it is not the encrypting device itself.

Analogy

Think of the CGW as a contact card in AWS that stores the address and routing preference for your on‑prem VPN device. AWS uses this contact card to choose where to send tunnel setup traffic and how to build configuration files.

Common confusion

Do not confuse the CGW resource with the physical device's configuration. You still manage encryption, PSKs, and tunnel IPs on your device.

screens.title: Static Routing vs Dynamic (BGP)
screens.narratorSegment: Static routing and dynamic routing with BGP are the two primary choices for routing across a Site‑to‑Site VPN. Static routing means you manually tell AWS which on‑prem CIDRs are reachable through the VPN, and you configure reciprocal static routes on your on‑prem device to reach VPC CIDRs. It is straightforward and may be acceptable for simple or test networks, but it lacks automatic failover. If one of the two IPsec tunnels goes down, traffic could still be sent to that tunnel until someone updates routes or the tunnel recovers. In contrast, BGP automates route advertisement and withdrawal: the VGW advertises VPC CIDRs and your device advertises on‑prem CIDRs. When a tunnel fails, BGP withdraws the affected routes and traffic shifts to the healthy tunnel without manual intervention. BGP requires an ASN on both sides — AWS uses a private ASN for VGWs — and your device must support BGP. A common misconception is that BGP always requires complex configuration; in many cases the BGP setup is a small addition that dramatically improves operational resilience. For production deployments, prefer BGP for automatic failover and simplified route management.

keyIdea.text: Static routing is simple but manual; BGP adds initial complexity but provides automatic route propagation and failover.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Static vs BGP
Comparison

Static Routing

  • Manual route entries on both AWS and on‑prem device.
  • Simple to configure for small, stable networks.
  • No automatic withdrawal on tunnel failure — manual intervention needed.

Dynamic Routing (BGP)

  • Automatic route advertisement and withdrawal between your device and the VGW.
  • Supports automatic failover when one tunnel fails.
  • Requires a unique on‑prem BGP ASN and device support for BGP.
Concrete scenario

If your on‑prem network is 10.0.0.0/16 and your VPC is 172.31.0.0/16, static routing requires entering those CIDRs on both sides. With BGP, once the neighbor forms, routes are exchanged automatically and updated if links change.

Misconception

BGP is not inherently risky; it introduces a manageable protocol setup that yields reliable automated failover when configured correctly.

Key Takeaway

Prefer BGP for production to gain automatic route failover; use static only for simple or short‑lived setups.

screens.title: Required CGW Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: When you create a Customer Gateway in AWS you must provide a small set of parameters that determine how AWS will attempt to connect to your device. The most critical is the public IP address of the on‑prem VPN device. This must be a static, internet‑routable IP reachable from AWS; if your device sits behind NAT you must ensure NAT‑T and correct external IP addressing and port forwarding. The second key value is the BGP ASN. If you plan to use dynamic routing, provide your on‑prem ASN so BGP adjacency can be established with the Virtual Private Gateway. If you choose static routing, the ASN field is still required but serves as a placeholder — you can enter an arbitrary valid ASN such as 65000. Finally, supply a device name as a descriptive label to help teams identify the CGW resource. A frequent operational pitfall is entering a dynamic or incorrect public IP; because AWS uses this value to target tunnel negotiations, any mismatch prevents tunnel establishment. Always confirm the external IP matches what AWS can reach and document the ASN used for BGP configuration.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Required CGW Parameters
Core Fields

What to enter when creating a CGW

These values tell AWS where to send IKE and how routing will be handled.

Public IP
A static, internet‑routable address for your VPN device. If behind NAT, ensure NAT‑T and correct external mapping.
BGP ASN
Your on‑prem ASN for dynamic routing. If using static routing, AWS still requires a value as a placeholder.
Device name
A human label that helps with operations and configuration tracking.
Operational tip
Record the CGW public IP in your maintenance runbook and schedule changes in maintenance windows since IP changes break tunnels.
Example entry
Public IP: 203.0.113.10 • BGP ASN: 65001 • Device name: "DC1-CGW-1"
Misstep to avoid

Do not register a dynamic ISP IP as the CGW address; it will disrupt tunnels if the address changes without notice.

screens.title: IPsec Tunnel Properties: Phase 1 (IKE)
screens.narratorSegment: IPsec tunnel establishment begins with Phase 1, often called IKE. Phase 1 negotiates a secure control channel used to exchange keys and agree on security parameters. The parameters you must match exactly on your device and what AWS expects include the encryption algorithm (for example AES‑128 or AES‑256), the hashing algorithm (such as SHA1 or SHA256), the Diffie‑Hellman group (Group 2, Group 14, etc.), and the lifetime for the IKE SA (commonly 28800 seconds). If any of these settings differ between AWS and your on‑prem device you will see a failure during IKE negotiation and the tunnel will not progress to Phase 2. A common troubleshooting step is to download the AWS VPN configuration file for your connection and copy the Phase 1 values verbatim into your device. An operational nuance: different vendors name these parameters slightly differently, so map vendor names to the AWS-specified algorithms. Concrete example: set IKE encryption to AES‑256, IKE hash to SHA256, DH group 14, and lifetime 28800 seconds to match the AWS template. Always test a single tunnel, confirm IKE up, then configure the second tunnel for redundancy.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › IPsec Phase 1 (IKE)
Definition

Phase 1 (IKE)

Negotiates the secure control channel and agrees keys and algorithms used by Phase 2.

  • Encryption: AES‑128 or AES‑256
  • Hash: SHA1 or SHA256
  • DH group: Group 2, Group 14, etc.
  • Lifetime: commonly 28800 seconds
Example
IKE encryption AES‑256, IKE hash SHA256, DH group 14, lifetime 28800. Copy these from the AWS config and match them exactly on your device.
Common mistake

A mismatch in DH group or hash algorithm causes IKE negotiation to fail; logs will show Phase 1 errors.

Key Takeaway

Verify Phase 1 fields exactly against the AWS configuration to allow the tunnel to progress to Phase 2.

screens.title: IPsec Phase 2 (ESP) Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Phase 2 negotiates the actual IPsec parameters that protect user traffic once the secure control channel from Phase 1 is established. Typical Phase 2 settings you must align include the ESP encryption algorithm (AES‑128 or AES‑256), ESP hash algorithm (SHA1 or SHA256), whether Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) is used and which DH group it uses, and the IPsec SA lifetime (often 3600 seconds). PFS ensures that new keys are derived for each Phase 2 session using a DH exchange, which increases security but requires matching DH groups on both sides. If PFS is enabled on AWS but not on your device, Phase 2 will fail. Another critical piece for Phase 2 is the policy transform set or the IPsec profile name on your device — it must reference the agreed algorithms and any PFS settings. A concrete example: configure ESP encryption AES‑256, ESP hash SHA256, PFS group 14, lifetime 3600 seconds. Misconfigurations here typically produce Phase 2 negotiation failures visible in device logs; consult the AWS config output and mirror the values exactly to resolve those failures. IPsec Phase 2 (ESP) Parameters means phase 2 parameters encrypt user data; mismatched esp or pfs settings between aws and your device will prevent the tunnel from carrying traffic.. In practical terms, where data encryption and perfect forward secrecy are negotiated. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › IPsec Phase 2
Definition

Phase 2 (ESP)

Negotiates encryption and authentication for the actual IP packets carried by the tunnel.

  • ESP encryption: AES‑128 or AES‑256
  • ESP hash: SHA1 or SHA256
  • PFS DH group: Group 2 or 14 when required
  • Lifetime: commonly 3600 seconds
Example

ESP AES‑256 with SHA256, PFS Group 14, lifetime 3600. Put these values into your transform-set or IPsec profile exactly as AWS specifies.

Common mistake

Enabling PFS on one side and not the other will break Phase 2 negotiation — always mirror PFS settings.

Key Takeaway

Mirror AWS Phase 2 (ESP) settings exactly to allow encrypted traffic to flow through the tunnel.

screens.title: Pre-shared Keys, Tunnel IPs, and BGP Peering
screens.narratorSegment: Each tunnel receives a unique pre‑shared key from AWS used to authenticate the endpoints during IKE. You must configure the matching PSK on your device for each tunnel. AWS also assigns a pair of tunnel inside IPs — one for your device and one for the VGW — which are used either for static routing or as BGP peer addresses if you enable dynamic routing. When using BGP, you will configure your router to peer to the AWS tunnel IP and advertise your on‑prem CIDRs; AWS advertises the VPC CIDRs back to you. A concrete configuration sequence is: configure IKE and IPsec profiles, set the PSK for Tunnel1, assign the tunnel interface IP 169.254.20.2/30 on your device and expect 169.254.20.1/30 from AWS, then configure BGP with neighbor 169.254.20.1 remote‑as 64512 while your ASN is 65001. A common misconception is that a single PSK can be reused; AWS supplies unique PSKs per tunnel and you must use the correct one for each tunnel. Validate by checking tunnel up state and BGP adjacency or static route reachability. Pre-shared Keys, Tunnel IPs, and BGP Peering means each tunnel has its own psk and tunnel ip pair; those ips are the bgp peer addresses or the gateway for static routes.. In practical terms, how psks and tunnel addresses enable authentication and routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Each tunnel has its own PSK and tunnel IP pair; those IPs are the BGP peer addresses or the gateway for static routes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › PSK, Tunnel IPs, BGP
Explanation

AWS provides a PSK per tunnel and a pair of tunnel inside IPs. Set the PSK and tunnel IP on your device, then configure BGP to peer to the AWS tunnel IP if using dynamic routing.

Checkpoints
  • PSK matches exactly — typos cause auth failure.
  • Tunnel IPs used as neighbor addresses for BGP or next‑hop for static routes.
  • Unique PSK per tunnel — do not reuse unless AWS specifies.
Code walkthrough (example)
! --- Tunnel 1 ---
crypto isakmp key MyStrongPSK123 address 52.X.Y.Z no-xauth
interface Tunnel1
 ip address 169.254.20.2 255.255.255.252
 tunnel source GigabitEthernet0/0
 tunnel destination 52.X.Y.Z
!
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 169.254.20.1 remote-as 64512

  network 10.10.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0

This example maps the AWS-provided PSK and tunnel IPs into device commands; repeat for Tunnel 2 with its PSK and AWS IP.

screens.title: Configuring Two Redundant Tunnels
screens.narratorSegment: AWS provisions two independent IPsec tunnels to the VGW to provide resilience. Each tunnel terminates on a different AWS public IP and has its own unique PSK and tunnel inside IPs. Your on‑prem device must be configured for both tunnels so that failure of one path does not interrupt traffic. The typical workflow is: 1) Download the AWS VPN configuration for your connection and extract Tunnel1 and Tunnel2 parameters. 2) Configure Phase 1 and Phase 2 profiles on your device to match AWS values. 3) Configure Tunnel1 with its PSK and tunnel IP, test and confirm IKE and Phase 2 up. 4) Configure Tunnel2 with its PSK and tunnel IP and test. 5) Verify routing: if BGP is used check both neighbor relationships and route advertisements; if static routing ensure both tunnels have appropriate route entries and operational health checks if supported. A common operator error is configuring only one tunnel or copying the same PSK to both tunnels; both steps reduce redundancy or cause authentication problems. Always validate failover by simulating a tunnel down and confirming traffic shifts to the healthy tunnel.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Two Redundant Tunnels
Why two tunnels

AWS creates two tunnels with different public IPs and PSKs to provide path redundancy and enable failover.

Step checklist
  1. Download AWS VPN config and copy tunnel parameters.
  2. Create IKE/IPsec profiles matching AWS values.
  3. Configure Tunnel1, test, then configure Tunnel2.
  4. Validate routing and perform a failover test.
Example failure test

Bring down Tunnel1 and confirm that BGP withdraws affected routes or that traffic flows over Tunnel2 for static routing. If traffic is blackholed, recheck route configuration.

Pitfall

Avoid copying Tunnel1 settings onto Tunnel2; each tunnel must use its own PSK and AWS IP target.

Key Takeaway

Treat tunnels independently: configure and validate each with the AWS-supplied values and then test failover behavior.

screens.title: Common Configuration Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: There are several recurring mistakes that cause tunnels not to establish or to carry traffic incorrectly. First, mismatched IPsec parameters between AWS and your device — differing encryption, hash, DH group, or lifetimes — will stop Phase 1 or Phase 2 negotiations. The always-recommended practice is to download the AWS configuration and copy parameters verbatim. Second, incorrect Pre-shared Keys: a single character typo breaks authentication. Third, firewall or NAT issues: blocking UDP ports 500 and 4500 prevents IKE and NAT‑T; if your device is behind NAT ensure NAT‑T is enabled and that the public IP recorded in the CGW is the external NAT address. Fourth, routing misconfigurations: even with tunnels up, missing static routes or absent BGP advertisements will cause traffic to not reach the VPC or on‑prem networks. Fifth, using a dynamic public IP for the CGW: if the public IP changes, AWS will no longer be able to reach your device and the tunnels fail. For each mistake include a verification step such as checking IKE logs, verifying UDP reachability, confirming tunnel interface IPs, and inspecting BGP neighbor state or route tables.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Common Configuration Mistakes
Top mistakes
  • Mismatched IKE/IPsec parameters
  • Incorrect PSK entries
  • Blocked UDP ports 500 and 4500
  • NAT mapping issues and missing port forwarding
  • Routing configuration errors or missing BGP advertisements
Verification steps
  1. Check IKE and IPsec logs for negotiation errors.
  2. Confirm UDP 500/4500 reachability from AWS IPs.
  3. Validate tunnel interface IPs and BGP neighbor state or static route configuration.
Example: firewall blockage

If UDP 500 or 4500 is blocked between your device and AWS, IKE negotiation will not begin. Open these ports and test connectivity to the AWS VGW public IPs.

NAT nuance

If your device sits behind a NAT router, ensure NAT‑T is enabled and that the external address entered in the CGW matches the NAT’s public IP with appropriate port forwarding for 500/4500.

Warning

Changing the CGW public IP without reconfiguring AWS and your device breaks tunnels immediately; schedule such changes in maintenance windows.

screens.title: Verification and Troubleshooting Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: After configuration the verification steps are straightforward and should be scripted into your rollout. First, check reachability to the AWS VGW public IPs: ensure UDP 500 and 4500 are reachable from your device to those IPs. Second, inspect the IKE negotiation logs to confirm Phase 1 completes; look for successful SA establishment. Third, inspect Phase 2 logs and ensure the IPsec SA is established with the expected lifetime. Fourth, verify tunnel interface IPs are assigned and reachable; if using BGP, verify neighbor adjacency and the presence of VPC CIDRs in your device route table. Fifth, for static routing ensure static routes on both sides point to the correct tunnel interface or next hop. Sixth, simulate a tunnel failure and verify failover: with BGP you should see route withdrawal and traffic shift, with static routes you may need external checks or manual updates. Always keep PSKs and configuration files secure and perform changes in maintenance windows. A common diagnostic is to re-download the AWS VPN configuration and reconcile any discrepancy between it and your device settings. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will make the Customer Gateway concrete and useful. A Customer Gateway is the logical AWS record that represents your physical or virtual VPN device on premises. You’ll learn what fields AWS requires when you create that resource, how routing choices — static or BGP — affect resilience and operations, and which IPsec parameters your device must match to form tunnels. We will use a realistic on‑prem scenario with a BGP ASN and a public IP to show an actual configuration snippet, and we’ll cover common mistakes such as blocked UDP ports, mismatched encryption settings, NAT traversal pitfalls, and routing misconfigurations. By the end you will be able to prepare a generic IPsec configuration for most devices, know what AWS needs upfront, and validate basic tunnel and BGP state. Notice that the exercise emphasizes repeatable practices: always prefer a static public IP for the CGW resource, prefer BGP in production for automatic failover, and verify both IKE and IPsec parameters exactly against the AWS config file. Which part of the configuration feels most unfamiliar right now?

These objectives focus on core, verifiable skills. First, you will be able to explain the role of a Customer Gateway and why AWS needs a reachable public IP and routing model. Second, you will identify and correctly populate the critical parameters when creating a CGW resource: public IP, BGP ASN, and a device label. Third, you will understand static routing fundamentals: when static routes are acceptable, how they are configured on both sides, and their limitations for failover. Fourth, you will prepare a basic IPsec Phase 1 and Phase 2 parameter set for an on‑prem device, recognizing which attributes must match AWS exactly. Each objective connects to safe operational practice: create CGW during design, prefer static routing only for simple or test setups, and validate every IKE/IPsec field. For example, if you list your on‑prem network CIDR to AWS for static routing, you must also configure the reciprocal static route on your device so traffic to the VPC is routed into the tunnel. These objectives are practical and testable — you should be able to fill a template configuration and explain why each field matters.

These secondary objectives focus on making configuration dependable in real environments. First, you will distinguish static routing from BGP on operational grounds: static routing is simple but brittle, while BGP requires ASN setup but automates route propagation and failover. Second, you will configure tunnel interface addresses and pre‑shared keys, understanding that each tunnel uses a unique PSK provided by AWS. Third, you will learn the key troubleshooting checks: open UDP ports 500 and 4500, NAT‑T behavior if your device is behind NAT, and route advertisement validation. Fourth, you will prepare a template snippet for a generic IPsec device and translate AWS VPN config values into device commands. Each objective includes a verification step: check tunnel negotiation state, confirm BGP adjacency or static route reachability, and test traffic flow to the VPC. For example, after configuring BGP you should see the AWS‑advertised VPC CIDR in your device's route table; if not, verify neighbor configuration and that the tunnel IP addresses match the AWS config. These objectives make configuration testable and repeatable.

A Customer Gateway is a logical resource you create inside AWS to tell the platform where your on‑prem VPN device is and how it will behave. It does not perform encryption itself; the physical or virtual VPN appliance in your data center does that work. In practice, the CGW holds a small set of fields: the public IP address reachable from the internet, a BGP ASN if you plan to use dynamic routing, and an optional device name to help operators identify it. Why use a CGW resource? AWS needs to know the remote endpoint to allocate tunnel endpoints, produce configuration files, and establish the two independent IPsec tunnels that provide redundancy. A common misconception is treating the CGW as the tunnel — it’s not. Think of the CGW as a directory entry: it allows AWS to target the actual tunnel negotiations to your device. A concrete example: when you create a CGW with a public IP of 203.0.113.10 and ASN 65001, AWS will use that IP to start IKE negotiations and, if BGP is used, expect a BGP neighbor formed with the VGW. Key takeaway: keep the CGW's public IP stable and accurate; changing it will break existing tunnels and require reconfiguration.

Static routing and dynamic routing with BGP are the two primary choices for routing across a Site‑to‑Site VPN. Static routing means you manually tell AWS which on‑prem CIDRs are reachable through the VPN, and you configure reciprocal static routes on your on‑prem device to reach VPC CIDRs. It is straightforward and may be acceptable for simple or test networks, but it lacks automatic failover. If one of the two IPsec tunnels goes down, traffic could still be sent to that tunnel until someone updates routes or the tunnel recovers. In contrast, BGP automates route advertisement and withdrawal: the VGW advertises VPC CIDRs and your device advertises on‑prem CIDRs. When a tunnel fails, BGP withdraws the affected routes and traffic shifts to the healthy tunnel without manual intervention. BGP requires an ASN on both sides — AWS uses a private ASN for VGWs — and your device must support BGP. A common misconception is that BGP always requires complex configuration; in many cases the BGP setup is a small addition that dramatically improves operational resilience. For production deployments, prefer BGP for automatic failover and simplified route management.

When you create a Customer Gateway in AWS you must provide a small set of parameters that determine how AWS will attempt to connect to your device. The most critical is the public IP address of the on‑prem VPN device. This must be a static, internet‑routable IP reachable from AWS; if your device sits behind NAT you must ensure NAT‑T and correct external IP addressing and port forwarding. The second key value is the BGP ASN. If you plan to use dynamic routing, provide your on‑prem ASN so BGP adjacency can be established with the Virtual Private Gateway. If you choose static routing, the ASN field is still required but serves as a placeholder — you can enter an arbitrary valid ASN such as 65000. Finally, supply a device name as a descriptive label to help teams identify the CGW resource. A frequent operational pitfall is entering a dynamic or incorrect public IP; because AWS uses this value to target tunnel negotiations, any mismatch prevents tunnel establishment. Always confirm the external IP matches what AWS can reach and document the ASN used for BGP configuration.

IPsec tunnel establishment begins with Phase 1, often called IKE. Phase 1 negotiates a secure control channel used to exchange keys and agree on security parameters. The parameters you must match exactly on your device and what AWS expects include the encryption algorithm (for example AES‑128 or AES‑256), the hashing algorithm (such as SHA1 or SHA256), the Diffie‑Hellman group (Group 2, Group 14, etc.), and the lifetime for the IKE SA (commonly 28800 seconds). If any of these settings differ between AWS and your on‑prem device you will see a failure during IKE negotiation and the tunnel will not progress to Phase 2. A common troubleshooting step is to download the AWS VPN configuration file for your connection and copy the Phase 1 values verbatim into your device. An operational nuance: different vendors name these parameters slightly differently, so map vendor names to the AWS-specified algorithms. Concrete example: set IKE encryption to AES‑256, IKE hash to SHA256, DH group 14, and lifetime 28800 seconds to match the AWS template. Always test a single tunnel, confirm IKE up, then configure the second tunnel for redundancy.

Phase 2 negotiates the actual IPsec parameters that protect user traffic once the secure control channel from Phase 1 is established. Typical Phase 2 settings you must align include the ESP encryption algorithm (AES‑128 or AES‑256), ESP hash algorithm (SHA1 or SHA256), whether Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) is used and which DH group it uses, and the IPsec SA lifetime (often 3600 seconds). PFS ensures that new keys are derived for each Phase 2 session using a DH exchange, which increases security but requires matching DH groups on both sides. If PFS is enabled on AWS but not on your device, Phase 2 will fail. Another critical piece for Phase 2 is the policy transform set or the IPsec profile name on your device — it must reference the agreed algorithms and any PFS settings. A concrete example: configure ESP encryption AES‑256, ESP hash SHA256, PFS group 14, lifetime 3600 seconds. Misconfigurations here typically produce Phase 2 negotiation failures visible in device logs; consult the AWS config output and mirror the values exactly to resolve those failures. IPsec Phase 2 (ESP) Parameters means phase 2 parameters encrypt user data; mismatched esp or pfs settings between aws and your device will prevent the tunnel from carrying traffic.. In practical terms, where data encryption and perfect forward secrecy are negotiated. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Each tunnel receives a unique pre‑shared key from AWS used to authenticate the endpoints during IKE. You must configure the matching PSK on your device for each tunnel. AWS also assigns a pair of tunnel inside IPs — one for your device and one for the VGW — which are used either for static routing or as BGP peer addresses if you enable dynamic routing. When using BGP, you will configure your router to peer to the AWS tunnel IP and advertise your on‑prem CIDRs; AWS advertises the VPC CIDRs back to you. A concrete configuration sequence is: configure IKE and IPsec profiles, set the PSK for Tunnel1, assign the tunnel interface IP 169.254.20.2/30 on your device and expect 169.254.20.1/30 from AWS, then configure BGP with neighbor 169.254.20.1 remote‑as 64512 while your ASN is 65001. A common misconception is that a single PSK can be reused; AWS supplies unique PSKs per tunnel and you must use the correct one for each tunnel. Validate by checking tunnel up state and BGP adjacency or static route reachability. Pre-shared Keys, Tunnel IPs, and BGP Peering means each tunnel has its own psk and tunnel ip pair; those ips are the bgp peer addresses or the gateway for static routes.. In practical terms, how psks and tunnel addresses enable authentication and routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AWS provisions two independent IPsec tunnels to the VGW to provide resilience. Each tunnel terminates on a different AWS public IP and has its own unique PSK and tunnel inside IPs. Your on‑prem device must be configured for both tunnels so that failure of one path does not interrupt traffic. The typical workflow is: 1) Download the AWS VPN configuration for your connection and extract Tunnel1 and Tunnel2 parameters. 2) Configure Phase 1 and Phase 2 profiles on your device to match AWS values. 3) Configure Tunnel1 with its PSK and tunnel IP, test and confirm IKE and Phase 2 up. 4) Configure Tunnel2 with its PSK and tunnel IP and test. 5) Verify routing: if BGP is used check both neighbor relationships and route advertisements; if static routing ensure both tunnels have appropriate route entries and operational health checks if supported. A common operator error is configuring only one tunnel or copying the same PSK to both tunnels; both steps reduce redundancy or cause authentication problems. Always validate failover by simulating a tunnel down and confirming traffic shifts to the healthy tunnel.

There are several recurring mistakes that cause tunnels not to establish or to carry traffic incorrectly. First, mismatched IPsec parameters between AWS and your device — differing encryption, hash, DH group, or lifetimes — will stop Phase 1 or Phase 2 negotiations. The always-recommended practice is to download the AWS configuration and copy parameters verbatim. Second, incorrect Pre-shared Keys: a single character typo breaks authentication. Third, firewall or NAT issues: blocking UDP ports 500 and 4500 prevents IKE and NAT‑T; if your device is behind NAT ensure NAT‑T is enabled and that the public IP recorded in the CGW is the external NAT address. Fourth, routing misconfigurations: even with tunnels up, missing static routes or absent BGP advertisements will cause traffic to not reach the VPC or on‑prem networks. Fifth, using a dynamic public IP for the CGW: if the public IP changes, AWS will no longer be able to reach your device and the tunnels fail. For each mistake include a verification step such as checking IKE logs, verifying UDP reachability, confirming tunnel interface IPs, and inspecting BGP neighbor state or route tables.

After configuration the verification steps are straightforward and should be scripted into your rollout. First, check reachability to the AWS VGW public IPs: ensure UDP 500 and 4500 are reachable from your device to those IPs. Second, inspect the IKE negotiation logs to confirm Phase 1 completes; look for successful SA establishment. Third, inspect Phase 2 logs and ensure the IPsec SA is established with the expected lifetime. Fourth, verify tunnel interface IPs are assigned and reachable; if using BGP, verify neighbor adjacency and the presence of VPC CIDRs in your device route table. Fifth, for static routing ensure static routes on both sides point to the correct tunnel interface or next hop. Sixth, simulate a tunnel failure and verify failover: with BGP you should see route withdrawal and traffic shift, with static routes you may need external checks or manual updates. Always keep PSKs and configuration files secure and perform changes in maintenance windows.
